To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
families with Li-Fraumenie syndrome carrying mutations in the TP53 gene that alter the DNA binding domain show a higher cancer incidence than families with other types of TP53 mutation.

1) the cancer phenotype in Li-Fraumenie syndrome is correlated with the genotype of the TP53 mutation, 2) families with mutations in the core domain of the TP53 gene have a higher cancer risk than families with mutations outside the core domain or with no mutation, and 3) the cancer phenotype associated with missense mutations is consistent with the observation that these mutations exhibit gain of functional activity and/or dominant negative properties in experimental systems.

(i) Li-Fraumenie families with germline mutations in the core domain of the TP53 gene have a higher incidence of cancer, and earlier age at diagnosis of cancer, than other families; (ii) the cancers in these families show loss of the wild type TP53 allele in a smaller proportion than in other families; (iii) the cancers of these families have a higher proportion of mutations in the core region of the p53 gene, than other cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterisation of cancer predisposition genes.
the identification of genes that predispose to cancer, the elucidation of their role in the pathogenesis of cancer, and the development of new strategies for cancer prevention and treatment.
the identification of genetic factors which contribute to cancer predisposition in the general population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cancer phenotype of Li-Fraumenii families is influenced by the type of TP53 mutation.
the Li-Frauman syndrome is caused by a TP53 germline mutation and the type of mutation is important in determining cancer phenotype.
TP53 mutation status does not predict cancer risk, as the risk is determined by the mutation itself and by the environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Li-Fraumensy cancer predisposition syndrome, which is caused by germline TP 53 mutations, is characterized by a highly penetrant cancer incidence.
the cancer phenotype in Li-Fraumenie patients is associated with their germline TP3 genotype and that certain TP53 mutations confer a more aggressive cancer phenotype.
TP53 missense mutations in families with Li-Fraumenie syndrome are associated with a higher cancer incidence, and earlier ages at cancer diagnosis, than other mutations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Li-Fraumani syndrome is associated with a high risk of developing a wide range of cancers, including soft tissue sarcomas, brain tumours and breast cancers.

the Li-Frauman syndrome (LFS) is a highly heterogeneous syndrome, which is characterized by a wide spectrum of cancer predisposition, and that the cancer predisposition in LFS is strongly correlated with the type of TP53 mutation.

the Li-Fraumanis cancer predisposition syndrome, associated with germlin TP53 mutation, is associated with a more highly penetrance phenotype when the mutation is missense, compared with protein-truncating or other inacti-vating mutations.
